newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. rights monitors report killings in Rwanda. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.N. rights monitors report killings in Rwanda. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]

text.p: United Nations human rights monitors in Rwanda have received reports of Rwandan refugees returning home from Zaire killing "people described as genocide survivors", a U.N. spokeswoman said on Tuesday.
(Corrects to make clear reports refer to returning refugees doing the killing.)

The spokeswoman said Javier Zuniga, head of the U.N. Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda, called for thorough investigation of the incidents and for follow-up action "in order to develop confidence in the rule of law and (to) avoid increasing tensions."

The field operation -- the United Nations' largest human rights programme -- deploys 119 officers throughout Rwanda, where 500,000 Hutu refugees have returned in the last two weeks from eastern Zaire.
Ethnic tensions are running high in Rwandan villages where wounds are still fresh among Tutsi survivors of the Hutu-led 1994 genocide.

Houses of many returnees have been occupied by Tutsis and diplomats fear reprisals and arbitrary arrests of Hutus. They say that, in some cases, Tutsis have falsely accused returnees of participating in the ethnic slaughter so as to retain property..

"Human rights field officers have been receiving reports of incidents in which people have been killed. In several cases returnees are accused of killing people described as genocide survivors," U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut told a news briefing in Geneva.

"The head of the (U.N.) operation believes it is essential that these incidents are quickly and thoroughly investigated and acted upon in order to develop confidence in the rule of law and avoid increasing tensions," she added.
She had no further detail from preliminary reports.
Jose Ayala-Lasso, U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, is due to arrive in Kigali on Thursday for a three-day mission.
It is his fourth visit to Rwanda.
(Corrects from "...his first visit to the U.N.'s largest human rights field operation", Gastaut said.)
Ayala-Lasso, a former Ecuadorean diplomat, will travel to areas which have received large numbers of returnees and meet senior governmental officials and local rights groups.
A week ago U.N. human rights observers reported that some 500,000 Rwandans had gone home to their country from eastern Zaire and their situation was "generally satisfactory".

Most returnees had arrived back in their native villages and communes, where local authorities were asking that soldiers of the former government army announce themselves and be registered, U.N. officals said at the time.
Some 500 ex-soldiers had been registered and 21 people arrested as of November 23.

But in most cases they appear to heve have been detained for their own security -- to avoid attacks by genocide survivors who suspect them of involvement in killings, according to the U.N. field team.
Ayala-Lasso has called for the number of observers in Rwanda to be increased to 150 by the end of the year. He is also seeking $29 million to finance a total of 300 observers during 1997.
